hook: The "Dumb Ox" who became the greatest thinker of medieval Europe.

pages.x: Thomas was born around 1225 in the castle of Roccasecca in Italy, to a noble family who expected him to become an abbot. When he joined the Dominicans, a new order of poor preaching friars, his brothers kidnapped him and kept him locked in the family castle for a year.

In Cologne he studied with Albert the Great. Big, quiet and slow, he was nicknamed "the Dumb Ox" by the other students. Albert told them: "You call him the Dumb Ox, but one day his bellowing will be heard all over the world."

He taught at the University of Paris, the greatest school of the age, and could dictate to several secretaries at once. At a dinner with King Louis IX he sat silent, then banged the table and cried: "That settles the Manichees!" He had been working out an argument all through the meal.

His great work, the Summa Theologica, asks thousands of questions, from "Does God exist?" to "Can an angel be in two places at once?", and answers each by first setting out the best arguments against his own view. It offers five ways to prove that God exists.

Many Christians feared the newly rediscovered works of Aristotle. Thomas showed they could fit with Christian belief: faith and reason both come from God, so they cannot truly disagree. His ideas on natural law and just war still shape ethics and law.

In December 1273, after a vision during Mass, he stopped writing. "All that I have written seems like straw compared with what I have seen." He died a few months later, aged about 49, and was made a saint in 1323.
Aquinas is the leading theologian of the Catholic Church. His joining of faith and reason still shapes Catholic teaching, and his writing on natural law shaped Western ideas of justice.
pts: Joined Aristotle's philosophy with Christian faith
